title: The Sunday evening psalm (Psalm 109 [110])
hookLine: the psalm that opens Sunday Vespers, about a priest forever like Melchisedech
tomorrow: From the rising of the sun (Psalm 112 [113])

lines: A BELL, AND THE MONKS FILE IN.
cards: Sunday, late afternoon, the light going gold. In a monastery, a bell rings, and the monks file into their stalls, facing each other across the choir. In a cathedral side chapel, a handful of people gather.

In a city apartment, someone opens an app. All about to pray the Church's evening prayer at the same hour. And every Sunday, week after week, it begins with the same psalm, about a king and a very mysterious priest.

teach.b: The evening prayer is called Vespers, from the Latin vesper, evening, the same word for the evening star. With Lauds in the morning, it's one of the two great hinges of the Church's daily prayer.
It gathers up the day and offers it back, often with incense rising and a candle lit.

teach.h: SIT THOU AT MY RIGHT HAND.
teach.b: Sunday Vespers opens with Psalm 109 in the Douay, 110 in most Bibles: "The Lord said to my Lord: Sit thou at my right hand: Until I make thy enemies thy footstool." It's a royal psalm, a king being enthroned.
Jesus puzzled his listeners with it. Matthew says he asked, "What think you of Christ? whose son is he?" David's, they said.
Then how can David call him my Lord?

"If David then call him Lord, how is he his son?" No one could answer him a word. The New Testament comes back to this psalm again and again, hearing in it the risen Christ seated at God's right hand.
Then the strangest line: "The Lord hath sworn, and he will not repent: Thou art a priest for ever according to the order of Melchisedech."
Melchisedech appears in Genesis for just a few verses: a king of Salem who comes out to meet Abraham, "bringing forth bread and wine, for he was the priest of the most high God," and blesses him.
Genesis gives him no family tree. The Letter to the Hebrews makes much of that, calling him without beginning of days or end of life, and builds its picture of Christ's priesthood on him.
Catholics still hear his name in the Roman Canon, the first Eucharistic Prayer, and this psalm can be sung when priests are ordained: a priest for ever.

how: Catholics who pray the Liturgy of the Hours say Vespers (Evening Prayer) at the end of the day, and on every Sunday it opens with Psalm 109 [110]; in cathedrals and monasteries it is often sung, sometimes with incense.

games.q: you're one of Jesus's listeners. he asks: if David calls the Christ my Lord, how is he David's son? what happens?
o: no one can answer him a word.
they change the subject to taxes.
games.why: Matthew says no man was able to answer him a word, and from that day no one dared ask him any more questions.

practice: Picture the light fading at the end of today, and look back over the day: what it held, what it cost, what you'd hand back.
If you pray, offer the day to God the way Vespers does, perhaps with a line from a psalm you've learned; if you don't, simply watch the light change in your mind, and let the day end.
